text: Abortion (fetal loss between day 35 and day 110 of gestation, with fetus expulsion) can follow any high-fever infectious disease (>41°C, e.g. CSF, Erysipelas), though it isn't a defining feature of those diseases. In Cambodia, a high abortion rate specifically points to a few causes. PRRS: sows off feed for 7–10 days, fever up to 41°C, abortion rates reaching 50% over 4–6 weeks, occurring at any gestation stage but mostly late, with sow mortality potentially over 10% during this period. Leptospirosis: usually introduced via urine from carrier pigs (often not visibly sick) or occasionally rodents, spreading pig-to-pig or via contaminated feed/water; hard to eliminate once established. Signs: anorexia and fever 2–6 days before abortion; sows/gilts abort within 1–3 weeks of the expected farrowing date, or deliver a litter of dead, full-term piglets; necropsy of newborns shows excess fluid/fibrin in the abdominal cavity and sometimes jaundice. Treatment: a single streptomycin dose (25 mg/kg) clears most infected pigs — recommended for any newly introduced pig; Tetracycline (ideally combined with Tylosin) mixed in feed for 2 weeks helps control it on an affected farm. Mycotoxins: from corn harvested late or under-dried (undetectable without lab testing) — sows vomit, then abort about 2 days later. Dexamethasone: injecting it during the last 3 weeks of gestation itself causes abortion, so it should be avoided in late-pregnancy sows.
